D:\\wt\\enhc01\\vlog\\enhc01\\voz\\b000_.text: You're standing on a car lot. It's 91 degrees. The asphalt is soft under your shoes. And a young man in a white shirt is walking toward you with his hand already out. He's smiling. He's going to ask you a question. A friendly little question. And the second you answer it, he knows exactly how much extra he can charge you. I know. Because for 40 years, I was that young man. My name is Hector. I sold cars in Miami from 1975 to 2015. First on the lot, then in the finance office in the back. Today I'm going to give you the 10 questions we asked every senior who walked onto that lot, what we did with your answer, and the exact sentence you say back. And the last one, number 10, is the one nobody does. Not my friends, not my neighbors, nobody. Stay for that one. Okay. let me tell you who you're talking to

D:\\wt\\enhc01\\vlog\\enhc01\\voz\\b001_.text: I came to Miami in 1966, 12 years old, on the Freedom flights from Havana. My father fixed refrigerators on Calle Ocho. And in 1975, I got a job on the lot at Coral Way Motors, on Coral Way, selling used cars in a polyester tie that honestly should have been illegal. Then from 89 to 2015, I was the finance manager at Bird Road Auto Plaza, the little office in the back. We called it The Box. That's where the real money is made. I'll get to that. I retired in 2015. My wife Marisol says I retired from lying. That's not fair, but it's not completely wrong either. And now I'm on your side of the desk. I don't sell anything anymore. I owe you this and you'll understand why when I tell you about Mrs. Shapiro. My first boss was a man named Abe Feldman, sales manager at Coroway Motors.

D:\\wt\\enhc01\\vlog\\enhc01\\voz\\b002_.text: Short man, go watch. Always a cigar he never lit. The first day, he sat me down with a yellow legal pad and he said, Hector, the customer who talks the most pays the most. That's it. That was the training. Everything I'm going to tell you today comes from that one sentence. Every question on a car lot has one job to get you talking. So let's start. Question number one. What brings you in today? Sounds nice, right? Like a waiter. But that question is not about you. It's about your clock. The salesman wants to know one thing. How fast do you need a car? Because a person who needs a car tomorrow pays more than a person who needs a car someday. August 1992. Hurricane Andrew. If you were in Miami, you remember. Homestead, Cutler Ridge, Florida City, flattened. Thousands of cars crushed under roofs and trees.

D:\\wt\\enhc01\\vlog\\enhc01\\voz\\b003_.text: And the week after the storm, people came up South Dixie Highway to the dealerships with their insurance checks in an envelope. No car, no power at home, kids sleeping at the Cousins in Westchester. And the first thing they heard was, what brings you in today? And they told the truth. My car is under my neighbor's carport, under the carport. I need something by Monday so I can get to work. I was in the box by then, at Bird Road. And I watched the sales managers that month. No discounts, not one, sticker price, plus every add-on, because they knew the customer had told them. My clock is broken, and a broken clock pays retail. So what do you say back? You don't lie, you just don't hand over the clock. You say, I'm comparing a few cars, and I'm buying this month from whoever gives me the best out-the-door price. That's it. Now he doesn't know if you need it tomorrow or in four weeks.

D:\\wt\\enhc01\\vlog\\enhc01\\voz\\b004_.text: And every week he's not sure, he gets a little nicer. And if your car really did die, you still say the same thing. Rent a car for three days if you have to. A rental for three days is $150. A desperate customer is $2,000, $3,000. The rental is cheaper every single time. Question number two, and this is the big one, the one Abe loved. What kind of monthly payment are you looking for? Let me show you what Abe drew on that yellow pad in 1975. He took a pen and drew a cross. Four boxes. We called it the four square. Top left, the price of the car. Top right, your trade-in. Bottom left, your down payment. Bottom right, the monthly payment. And Abe said, Hector, the customer can only watch one box at a time. Find the box he's watching and make your money in the other three. And the box most seniors watch is the payment.

D:\\wt\\enhc01\\vlog\\enhc01\\voz\\b005_.text: Because you live on a fixed income, right? Social Security on the third, the pension on the first. You know exactly what fits. So when he asks, what payment are you looking for? You say, oh, around $500. And that's the most expensive sentence you will say all year. Here's why. Let's say the car is $30,000 at 6.9%. For 60 months, 5 years, that's about $593 a month. Too much, you said $500. So I don't lower the price. I stretched the loan. 84 months, 7 years. Now it's about $451. You're happy. You're under $500, but you just paid about $2,350 more in interest. And I still have almost $50 a month of room under your $500. You know what I do with $50 a room? I put a service contract in it.

D:\\wt\\enhc01\\vlog\\enhc01\\voz\\b006_.text: $2,000 of extras on an 84-month loan is only about $30 a month. You don't even feel it. That's called payment packing. I did it for 26 years. I'm not proud of it. And I'll tell you something else about the seven-year loan. You're 70. The loan ends when you're 77. Most people trade the car before the loan is done. And on a long loan, for years you owe more than the car is worth. They call it being upside down. and the dealer is happy to roll that balance into your next car. And the next one, Abe had a word for those customers, annuities. He meant it as a compliment. So what do you say back? Every time, word for word, I don't shop by the payment. What's the out-the-door price? Out-the-door means everything. The car, the taxes, the tag, every fee, one number. And if he says, well, it depends on your payment, you say it again.

D:\\wt\\enhc01\\vlog\\enhc01\\voz\\b007_.text: Same words, same convoys. I don't shop by the payment. What's the out-the-door price? He'll get it. Eventually, he always gets it. Now, before I give you question three, I have to tell you about a lady. Because she's the reason I'm sitting here. April 1988, Coral Way Motors. A lady walks onto the lot in a pink cardigan. In April, in Miami. Her name was Mrs. Dottie Shapiro. She lived off Kendall Drive near the Dalen Mall. 74 years old. Her husband Irving had passed that winter and she drove in his car, a big brown four-door sedan with a cracked dashboard and his reading glasses still in the cup holder. She told me that. His glasses were still in there. She couldn't move them and she answered every question I asked. Every single one. What brings you in? My Irving died and I don't trust his car. What payment?

D:\\wt\\enhc01\\vlog\\enhc01\\voz\\b008_.text: Whatever you think is fair, Hector, I'll tell you what happened to Mrs. Shapiro a piece at a time, because honestly, I can't tell it all at once. But I'll tell you this today, that afternoon, she was the easiest sale of my life, and I have regretted it for 38 years. Question number three, are you going to be trading in a vehicle today? Simple question, yes or no. But remember the four square, the trade is one of the four boxes, And when the dealer knows there's a trade, he can move money between the boxes like a man playing those three cups on the street on Flagler. Here's how it works. You want a good price on the new car. So I give you a beautiful price on the new car. $2,000 off. You're thrilled. And then I give you $2,000 less for your trade than it's worth. You walk out feeling like a champion and you paid exactly the same. Or the other way.

D:\\wt\\enhc01\\vlog\\enhc01\\voz\\b009_.text: I give you a fat number for your trade, more than it's worth, and I just don't move on the price of the new one. Same money, different box. So you say, let's settle the price of the new car first, as if I don't have a trade. Then we'll talk about whether I have one. Two separate deals, never one. And here's what my nephew Danny tells me. Danny sells today at a dealership in Douro. He says now people come in with a printout from the internet, the online value of their trade. Good, that's good. But the dealer will look at that number and say, oh that's the private party number, we can't pay that. So get two or three real written offers before you go. There are places that will buy your car outright and write you a check and they'll give you the offer on paper. Good for about a week. Bring that paper. Now your trade is not a guess, it's a number with a name on it. Question number four.

D:\\wt\\enhc01\\vlog\\enhc01\\voz\\b010_.text: Can I have your keys? Our used car manager just wants to take a quick look at your trade. Ten minutes, he says. Just a quick look. This one sounds so innocent. And it's one of the oldest tricks on the lot. 1981, Coral Way Motors. There was a salesman on our lot. I won't say his name. He's still alive and he goes to my church. He used to take the customer's keys and the keys would disappear, lost. The used car manager has them. He's on the phone. He's at lunch. and the customer sits in that little chair for two hours, three hours with a cold coffee because he can't leave, his car is out there and he can't drive it home. We had a name for that. We called it locking up the customer. Now most dealers today won't hide your keys for three hours, but they will hold them. And while they hold your keys, they hold your exit.

D:\\wt\\enhc01\\vlog\\enhc01\\voz\\b011_.text: And the exit is the only power you have on a car lot. The only one. So when he says, can I have your keys? You say, sure, you can look at it right now while I stand here. And then I like my keys back. Walk out with him. Watch him look at the car. He looks at the tires, the dashboard. He starts it. He drives it around the block. Fine. Then the keys go back in your pocket. Your pocket. Not on his desk. Question number five. Can I make a copy of your driver's license? It's just for the test drive. Now this one is partly true. A lot of dealers do copy your license for the test drive, for their insurance. And that's okay. I do it too. Somebody's driving my car. I want to know who. But here's what I saw happen many, many times at Bird Road. The copy of the license went to the sales desk. And sometimes with the license, there was a little form.

D:\\wt\\enhc01\\vlog\\enhc01\\voz\\b012_.text: A one-page thing you signed on the clipboard. You thought it was for the test drive. It was a credit application. And once they pull your credit, they know everything. Your score, how much you owe, what your last car payment was. They know your box better than you do. And there's a word for what happens next in the finance office. But I'm saving that for the next video. Because that's where I worked and that's where the real money is. Danny says now they have a tablet at the front desk. You type your name and your phone for the free coffee and you agree to the terms. Read the terms. Sometimes it says they can check your credit. So you say, you can copy my license for the test drive. You do not have my permission to run my credit. Say it nice. Say it with a smile. But say those words, permission to run my credit, and sign nothing on that clipboard that you didn't read twice. Nothing.

D:\\wt\\enhc01\\vlog\\enhc01\\voz\\b013_.text: And while we're talking about Danny, he told me about a new one last month and I almost spit out my coffee. You get a letter in the mail or a text message, Mr. Hernandez, we have a customer looking for your exact model, your exact color, and we'll pay top dollar. Come in this week and you think, oh, how nice. Somebody wants my car. There's no customer. There's a list. The dealer looks at who bought a car four or five years ago, who's almost done paying. and they invite you in to quote sell your car and when you get there the salesman says well while you're here let me show you the new one and you're back on the four square same questions same game so if you get that letter it's fine go but bring the 10 sentences and bring the paper with your other offers okay let me stop for a second because i know what you're thinking

D:\\wt\\enhc01\\vlog\\enhc01\\voz\\b014_.text: Hector, I'm 72. I don't want to fight with a 25-year-old in a white shirt. And you don't have to fight. That's the beautiful thing. Every sentence I'm giving you today is short and polite. You don't argue. You just don't give him the thing he asked for. That's all. And I promised you a couple from Hialeah who did exactly this to me. And they beat me. They beat me in my own office. You'll meet them in a minute. Question number six. How's your credit? Do you know your credit score? You'd think a good credit score is your friend. It is, but not if you say it out loud first. Here's something most people don't know, and I knew it every working day for 26 years. When you finance at the dealer, the dealer sends you application to a bank. The bank says, okay, this customer qualifies at, let's say, 5.9%. That's called the buy rate.

D:\\wt\\enhc01\\vlog\\enhc01\\voz\\b015_.text: And the dealer is often allowed to add on top of that, usually up to two, two and a half points. So the bank says 5.9, and I sit across from you in the box and I say, good news Mrs. Garcia, I got you approved at 7.9. And you say, thank you Hector. And that 2%, a big piece of it comes back to the dealership. We called it the reserve. On a $30,000 loan for six years, two extra points is a little over $2,000. for four minutes of my time and a handshake. So you don't tell them your score, you do something better. Before you ever go to the lot, you go to your bank or your credit union and you get pre-approved for a car loan. You walk in with a letter that says, approved up to 30,000 at 5.9, and when he asks, how's your credit? You say, I already have my financing. If you can beat my rate, I'll look at it.

D:\\wt\\enhc01\\vlog\\enhc01\\voz\\b016_.text: And I'll tell you what happens. Sometimes the dealer does beat it, really. Because now he has to. That's the only time I ever gave anybody the real buy rate. When they came in with a letter from the credit union on Bird Road and laid it on my desk like a royal flush. Question number seven. If I can get you to that number, will you buy the car today? Ah, this one is the hook. Abe called it the commitment. Because the salesman doesn't really decide anything. He's going to take your number to the sales manager in the tower, the little desk up high in the middle of the showroom where he can see everybody. And if you said yes, if you get me to that number, I'll buy today. Now you're locked. Now every number that comes back is close to your number and you said you'd buy. At Coral Way Motors, if a customer was getting cold, the salesman raised his hand and the manager came over.

D:\\wt\\enhc01\\vlog\\enhc01\\voz\\b017_.text: That was called the T.O., the turnover, a new face, a bigger title, a nicer watch. Abe was the T.O. He'd sit down. He'd put his cigar on the desk, and he'd say, listen to me. I'm the manager. I can do something special, but only today, only today. And people believed in only today. There's always another today. I sold cars on Christmas Eve and on the day after Christmas. There's always another today. So when he says, if I get you to that number, will you buy today? You say, if the numbers are right on paper, I'll consider it. I never decide at the desk. Then you go have a coffee. Go to the Versailles on Calle Ocho. Have a cafecito and a croqueta. Look at the paper and decide there. Away from the white shirt. The paper doesn't change when you leave the building. Only your feelings do. Now the couple from Hialeah. October 1996. Bird Road Auto Plaza. Mr. Mr.

D:\\wt\\enhc01\\vlog\\enhc01\\voz\\b018_.text: Rogelio Alvarez and his wife Nilda from Palm Avenue in Haleah. He had retired from Haleah Park, the racetrack, 31 years in the stables. She was a retired school secretary. And Mrs. Alvarez had a little notebook, blue spiral, the kind you buy at the drugstore. And in that notebook, she had written sentences like the ones I'm giving you today. The salesman asked, what payment are you looking for? And Mrs. Alvarez looked at a notebook and said, we don't shop by the payment. What's the out-the-door price? The salesman came to my office, I swear to God, and he said, Hector, these people have a notebook. And they walked out, twice. Two times they stood up, said thank you, and drove home to Haleah. And the third time they came back, she said three words to me, sitting in my own office, that I will never forget.

D:\\wt\\enhc01\\vlog\\enhc01\\voz\\b019_.text: I'll tell you those three words in a video coming later in this series, because they deserve their own video, believe me. Question number eight. So, what do you do? Are you working or are you retired? Sounds like small talk. On a car lot, there is no small talk. Everything is the four square. When you say retired, the salesman hears three things. Hears you have time. Hears you have savings, maybe. And hears you probably won't fight. That's what we thought. I'm sorry, but that's what we thought. And at Bird Road, there were salesmen who would go straight to the most expensive extras when the customer said retired. The paint protection, the fabric protection, the extended warranty for seven years on a 78-year-old customer. There's a whole video coming about why you should never tell a dealer your age. I'll give it the time it needs there.

D:\\wt\\enhc01\\vlog\\enhc01\\voz\\b020_.text: Today, just this. Your age and your job are not part of the price of a car. You can say, I'd rather not get into that. Let's talk about the car. Or if you want to be friendly, you can just say, oh, I keep busy. That's true for every retired person I know. Marisol keeps me very busy. And let me tell you about the snowbirds, because this is the same question in a different shirt. January 2004, a couple from New Jersey, winter condo in Sunny Isles, nice people. They come into Bird Road to buy a little car for the winter. And the salesman asks, so how long are you folks down here? And the husband says, oh, we fly back to Newark on Sunday. Sunday, it was Thursday. You see, that's question number one again. He just told us his clock, three days. and that car went out the door at almost full sticker with the window etching and the nitrogen because the salesman knew that

D:\\wt\\enhc01\\vlog\\enhc01\\voz\\b021_.text: If he didn't buy by Saturday, he'd have to come back next winter. So when someone asks how long you're in town, the answer is long enough to find the right car. Question number nine. What would it take to earn your business today? This is a beautiful question. It's open, it's humble, it's a trap. Because he wants you to say a number first. And whoever says the first number loses. Abe used to say that too. The first number is the anchor. and the whole negotiation swings around it like a boat in Biscayne Bay. Let's say the car is listed at $32,000 and you, a nice person, you say, well, I was thinking maybe $30,000. He goes to the tower, comes back with a long face, says, my manager says $31,500 is the absolute best. And you meet in the middle at $31,000 and you feel good. But maybe that car would have gone for $29,500. You never found out.

D:\\wt\\enhc01\\vlog\\enhc01\\voz\\b022_.text: Because you went first. So you say your best out-the-door price in writing with every fee listed line by line. That's what it would take. And then you stop talking. That part is the hardest. You stop talking. Remember what Abe said. The customer who talks the most pays the most. So the customer who talks the least, you get it. And when the paper comes back, read every line. Every line. Dealer fee, doc fee, the prep fee, the nitrogen in the tires, the etching on the windows. Some of those you can refuse and some you can't. And there's a whole video in this series about seven of them. But at least now you can see them. On paper you can see everything. In conversation you see nothing. Okay, we're at number ten, the one nobody does. Before I give it to you, I have to finish a little piece about Mrs. Shapiro. not the end just the next door

D:\\wt\\enhc01\\vlog\\enhc01\\voz\\b023_.text: That afternoon in April of 88, I had sold her a car. A nice little sedan, light blue, low miles. Good car, honestly. A fair price, more or less. And then Abe came to my desk and said, Hector, our finance man, Sal, is out with his gallbladder. You do the papers. And I took Mrs. Shapiro by the arm. She was a little unsteady in those white shoes. And I walked her to the back office. And she said, oh, the paperwork. Irving always did the paperwork. And I closed the door. That was my first month in the box. And what I did in that room is the thing I've never forgiven myself for. Next video. I promise. So. Question number 10. The one nobody does. The salesman is all smiles. You agreed on the car. You shook hands. And he says, wonderful. Now our finance manager is just going to go over a little paperwork with you. A little paperwork. And everybody says, okay, everybody.

D:\\wt\\enhc01\\vlog\\enhc01\\voz\\b024_.text: My smartest friends, retired engineers from Coral Gables, they all say okay and they follow him to the back. And that's the mistake because the finance office is not paperwork. The finance office is the second negotiation and it's the one where the dealer makes more money than on the car itself. At Bird Road, on a lot of deals, I made more in the box in 40 minutes than the salesman made on the whole car in 4 hours. So what nobody does is this. Before you walk into that office, before you stand up from the salesman's desk, you say, before I go in there, please print me the buyer's order with the out-the-door price and I'll sign it here. Then you hold that paper. That's your price.

D:\\wt\\enhc01\\vlog\\enhc01\\voz\\b025_.text: And when you sit down in the box and the finance man starts talking about protection plans and peace of mind and tire and wheel, you put that paper on his desk and you say anything that is not on this paper, the answer is no. And you smile. Nice. And you say no thank you as many times as he asks. And he will ask. I asked. I was very, very good at asking. And one more thing, because everybody gets this wrong. In Florida and in most states, there is no three-day cooling off period for a car you buy at the dealership. People think they have three days to change their mind. They don't. The federal cooling off rule has an exception for cars bought at the dealer's place of business. Once you sign in that office and drive off, it's done. So the no has to happen in the room, not at home in the kitchen the next morning. Let me give you all ten again, quick, so you can write them down.

D:\\wt\\enhc01\\vlog\\enhc01\\voz\\b026_.text: like Mrs. Alvarez in her blue notebook. One, what brings you in? You say, I'm comparing and I'm buying this month from whoever gives me the best out-the-door price. Two, what payment are you looking for? I don't shop by the payment. What's the out-the-door price? Three, do you have a trade? Let's settle the new car first as if I don't have one. Four, can I have your keys? Look at it now while I stand here and I'd like my keys back. 5. Can I copy your license? For the test drive, yes. You don't have my permission to run my credit. 6. How's your credit? I already have my financing. Beat my rate and I'll look. 7. If I get you to that number, will you buy today? If the numbers are right on paper, I'll consider it. I never decide at the desk. 8. What do you do? Are you retired? Let's talk about the car. 9. What would it take?

D:\\wt\\enhc01\\vlog\\enhc01\\voz\\b027_.text: Your best out-the-door price in writing. Every fee line by line. And then silence. And ten. The finance manager just wants to go over some paperwork. Print me the buyer's order. I'll sign it here. And anything that's not on this paper is a no. That's it. Ten sentences. You can put them on an index card in your wallet. Write them in big letters if your eyes are like mine. And one more sentence. A bonus. Because you stayed with me this long. The sentence to leave. because at some point, if the numbers are not right, you have to stand up. And that's hard for nice people. It was hard for Mrs. Shapiro. It's hard for my own sister and Coral Gables. So here it is. Thank you for your time. I'm going to think about it. Here's my phone number if the price changes. And you stand up. You don't explain. You don't apologize. If he says, wait, wait, let me talk to my manager, you can sit back down.

D:\\wt\\enhc01\\vlog\\enhc01\\voz\\b028_.text: That's fine. But if he says this price is only good today, you keep walking. Because I promise you from 40 years on that lot, the price is good tomorrow. The car will still be there tomorrow. And if it's not, there's another one exactly like it. Three miles down Bird Road. You know, people ask me, Hector, why are you doing this? 40 years, you made a good living. Your house in Westchester has paid off. And the truth is, for 40 years I was very good at a job that too many times hurt people who trusted me. Nice people, retired people, people like my mother would have been. And Abe used to say, the customer who talks the most pays the most. So now I'm the one talking. And this time it doesn't cost you anything. Now number 10 is the door to the box.

D:\\wt\\enhc01\\vlog\\enhc01\\voz\\b029_.text: And what happens inside that box, the 40 minutes, the menu, the pen, the speech I gave a thousand times, that's where the dealer really gets you. And there's one thing I did in that office to retirees almost every week. And it starts with the question so innocent you'll laugh. Are you paying cash? In the next video, I'm going to tell you, as a former finance manager, why a retiree should almost never walk in and just pay cash for a car. It sounds backwards. I know. A coach from Westchester learned it the hard way. And you'll hear what happened to Mrs. Shapiro when I closed that door. Subscribe so you don't miss it. And down in the comments, tell me what the dealer told you, the exact words, and I'll tell you if it's true. I read them all. Marisol says I read them instead of fixing the screen door. She's right. See you in the box.
